title: Notice pay vs garden leave - what employment contracts often get wrong
p1:
A resignation letter is not always the day an employee walks away.

Sometimes, the real question is: can the company stop you from working but still keep paying you?
p2:
Many employment contracts treat notice pay and garden leave as if they are the same thing. They are not.

Notice pay usually means an employee leaves immediately and receives payment instead of serving the notice period. Garden leave means the employee remains employed but is asked not to work during the notice period.
p3:
The surprising part? During garden leave, the employee may still have contractual obligations, such as confidentiality duties or restrictions on joining competitors, because the employment relationship continues.

A well-drafted contract should clearly explain when each option applies. Vague wording can create disputes about pay, duties, and post-employment restrictions.

The practical takeaway: never assume a clause called “notice period” tells the whole story. The exact wording can change what both sides can legally expect.
conclusion: Have you seen an employment contract that clearly explained the difference between notice pay and garden leave, or did it leave room for confusion?
